description: This course covers formal languages and automata theory, including finite automata, pushdown automata, Turing machines, and their respective languages. It explores regular expressions, context-free grammars, and the Chomsky hierarchy. Students will study the theory of computability, including the Church-Turing thesis, decidability, and the halting problem. The course also addresses complexity theory, including P vs NP, NP-completeness, and the Cook-Levin theorem. Topics include algorithmic complexity analysis, time and space complexity classes, and the application of computational theory in algorithm design and software verification. The course uses formal proofs, mathematical logic, and symbolic notation to analyze computational problems and their limits.

clos.text: Define the formal language classes in the Chomsky hierarchy, including regular languages, context-free languages, context-sensitive languages, and recursively enumerable languages.
Describe the operational semantics of finite automata, pushdown automata, and Turing machines, including their transition functions and acceptance criteria.
Explain the concept of decidability and undecidability, including the proof of the halting problem and its implications for computational limits.
Apply computational complexity analysis to classify problems into P, NP, and NP-complete categories using the Cook-Levin theorem.
Implement algorithms for parsing context-free grammars and verifying the correctness of formal proofs in computational theory.
